"Brow" has a few different meanings depending on what is being described.

This is the most common meaning. Your brow is the flat, smooth area of your face that sits above your eyebrows and below your hairline — what most people simply call the forehead.

"She wiped the sweat from her brow after the long run."
"He pressed a cool cloth against his brow to soothe the headache."

This meaning is very often used in literature and everyday speech whenever someone is describing a person's face, tiredness, worry, or physical effort.

"Brow" is also widely used to mean an eyebrow — the arch of hair that sits above each of your eyes. In this meaning, it usually appears in the singular ("brow") when referring to one eyebrow, or as "brows" for both.

"She raised a brow, clearly not believing what he said." (one eyebrow raised — a gesture of doubt or surprise)
"He furrowed his brows." (both eyebrows pulled together — a gesture of worry or deep thought)

Note that meanings 1 and 2 are closely linked because the eyebrows sit right on the lower edge of the forehead. This is why "brow" can refer to either the forehead as a whole or the eyebrows specifically — context will always make it clear which one is meant.
3. The Top Edge of a Hill or Slope

"Brow" can also describe the highest point of a hill or steep slope — specifically the rounded top edge just before the ground begins to fall away on the other side.

"The hikers finally reached the brow of the hill and saw the valley stretched out below them."
"A car suddenly appeared over the brow of the hill, coming fast toward us."

Think of it like the "forehead" of a hill — just as your forehead is the topmost flat part of your face before your head curves back, the brow of a hill is its topmost edge before it curves downward. The same word is used for both for exactly this visual reason.

Since this word appears in several well-known expressions, here are the important ones:

"By the sweat of one's brow" — This means through hard, physical work and personal effort. It suggests someone has worked so hard that they are literally sweating.

"He built his business by the sweat of his brow."

"A furrowed brow" — When someone's forehead is creased or wrinkled, it shows they are worried, concentrating hard, or confused. This is one of the most common ways "brow" appears in writing.

"She read the letter with a furrowed brow."

"To knit one's brows" — To pull the eyebrows together in a frown, showing concern or puzzlement.

"He knitted his brows as he tried to solve the problem."

"To raise a brow" (or "raise an eyebrow") — To lift one eyebrow slightly as a reaction, showing surprise, disbelief, or quiet skepticism.

"The expensive price tag raised a few brows."

The word "brow" always points to the idea of a top edge or upper boundary — whether it's the top of your face (forehead), the top of your eye (eyebrow), or the top of a hill. Once you hold that central idea in your mind, every use of the word will feel natural and logical.
